script.opening: “Hello, doctor. The health visitor came today and she told me to call you. I don’t know why really — I’m fine. I’m not depressed. I’m just on my own a lot.”

facts.topic: Why the health visitor was worried (if asked)
facts.text: “She asked me questions and I said I don’t go out much and sometimes I cry. That’s all.”
“Not sad all day. In the evenings I cry, when Kasun goes to work and it’s dark. I feel… useless. Like I’m not doing anything properly.” Started a few weeks after the birth.
“Anya makes me smile. When I talk to my mother on video, I laugh. I like cooking still.”
Sleeps when the baby sleeps; eats normally; tired, “but she feeds every three hours”. Concentration OK.
No thoughts of harming yourself or of ending your life. No thoughts of harming Anya — “never, she is my everything”. No hearing voices or strange beliefs. Bonding: “I love her so much.”
“I don’t know anyone. The bus with the pram is difficult, and I don’t like feeding her in front of people — at home in Sri Lanka, women stay at home with family after a baby.”

facts.topic: Her mother (if asked about family or support)
facts.text: “My mother was going to come for the first months — that is our custom, she would look after me. Her visa was refused.” Become tearful. “I feel I am doing it alone.”
“He is a good man. He works nights at a care home. In the day he sleeps. He doesn’t know I cry — I don’t want to worry him.”

facts.topic: Fear (only if the doctor asks what worries her about talking to doctors, or reassures about confidentiality)
facts.text: “If I say I have mental problems, will they take my baby? Will it be a problem for our visa?”
Bleeding stopped. No postnatal check with the GP — “nobody called me”. No contraception yet. Hair falling out a bit. Not taking any iron since hospital.
Graduate (accountancy). If asked about work: “I am allowed to work, but who would look after Anya?” Good English. Buddhist; there is a temple 40 minutes away. No alcohol or smoking.

Be polite, guarded and keen to show you are coping. Open up gradually if the doctor is warm and unhurried. Reveal the visa refusal and your fear about social services only if asked about support or about worries. Respond with relief to accurate reassurance. Accept a mix of practical support; you would rather talk to someone than take medicine.

ice.ideas: “I am not depressed — I am alone.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fears that admitting to mental health problems will lead to social services taking Anya or harm the family’s visas; grieving that her mother could not come for the postnatal period.
ice.expectations: To show the doctor she is coping so that “it doesn’t go further”.

cues: “I’m just on my own a lot.” — isolation is the real problem.
“I feel useless.” — low self-worth worth exploring.
“Her visa was refused.” — loss of expected support.

checkpoints.text: Uses the health visitor note and asks open questions about how she has been since the birth; explores why the health visitor was concerned

Assesses for depression and anxiety (low mood, anhedonia, sleep, appetite, energy, guilt, worthlessness) and risk: self-harm, suicidal thoughts, thoughts of harming the baby, psychotic features, bonding, past history
Explores support and context: husband’s night shifts, migration, mother’s visa refusal, cultural expectations of the postnatal period, barriers to going out
Explains a working understanding (adjustment reaction with isolation, not depression at present, but raised risk) and agrees watchful waiting with active support

Builds practical support: health visitor follow-up, Family Hub and baby groups, breastfeeding peer support and tips for feeding out, Home-Start, social prescriber, cultural community, NHS Talking Therapies, involving Kasun
Offers her postnatal check (FBC, ferritin, TSH for tiredness after PPH; contraception) and arranges follow-up in 2–3 weeks with clear safety-netting (NHS 111 mental health option, 999)
Finds and addresses her fear about social services and visas with accurate reassurance; respects her cultural expectations without stereotyping

worked.txt: “The health visitor wanted us to talk. I’m not here to label you — I’d just like to hear how things have really been since Anya arrived.”
“Some new mums have thoughts of harming themselves, or worries about harming their baby. Have you had any thoughts like that?”
“Sometimes people worry about what happens if they tell a doctor they’re struggling. Is anything like that on your mind?”
“Asking for help doesn’t lead to babies being taken away — Anya is clearly loved and thriving. And seeing a GP or getting support doesn’t affect your visa.”

“From what you’ve told me, I don’t think you’re depressed right now. I think you’re adjusting to a huge change — a new baby, a new country, and missing the help your mother would have given — very much on your own.”

f.learning: An EPDS score is a screening tool, not a diagnosis — assess properly. Use the Whooley questions (low mood, loss of interest) and a full risk assessment including self-harm, thoughts of harm to the baby, psychotic symptoms and bonding. An adjustment reaction is an expected, though distressing, response to a major stressor; it usually improves with support but raises the risk of later depression, so follow up. Isolation is a major driver of perinatal distress, especially for recent migrants whose expected family support is missing (many cultures have a structured postnatal rest period cared for by female relatives). Fear of social services or immigration consequences often silences women: be explicit that help-seeking does not lead to children being removed and does not affect visas. Visa dependants who have paid the immigration health surcharge have full NHS entitlement. Practical, local support (health visitor listening visits, Family Hubs, breastfeeding peer support, Home-Start, social prescribing, faith and cultural communities) and NHS Talking Therapies (which prioritises perinatal women) are first-line; medicines are not indicated for an adjustment reaction. Do not forget the woman’s own postnatal check — tiredness after a PPH warrants FBC and ferritin, and TSH for postpartum thyroiditis.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health: clinical management and service guidance (2014, updated 2020) · NICE NG194 Postnatal care (2021) · NHS England NHS 111 mental health option (2024)
knowledge.summary: Assess mood and risk properly, recognise an adjustment reaction with isolation, neutralise the fear about social services and visas, and build real support — with follow-up.

points.t: EPDS 10 or more suggests possible depression; 9 is below threshold but item content matters, as does clinical judgement. Whooley questions: during the past month, often bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless? By little interest or pleasure in doing things? Add GAD-2 for anxiety.

Self-harm and suicidal thoughts (suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in the first year), thoughts of harming the baby, psychotic symptoms (postpartum psychosis is an emergency — same-day perinatal mental health or crisis team), neglect, bonding, substance use, domestic abuse.

Emotional distress after an identifiable stressor, out of proportion or affecting functioning, without meeting criteria for depression. Management: support, problem-solving, social connection, talking therapy; review within weeks; escalate if symptoms worsen.

Health visitor listening visits; Family Hub and children’s centre groups; breastfeeding peer supporters and baby cafés (feeding covers, quieter spaces); Home-Start volunteers; social prescribing link worker; faith and cultural community groups; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral; perinatal peer support charities.

Dependants on work visas who have paid the immigration health surcharge can use the NHS like UK residents. Seeking help for mental health does not affect immigration status. Safeguarding referrals are made only when a child is at risk of harm — not because a parent is struggling.
Six-to-eight week maternal check: mood, bleeding, contraception, BP. Tiredness after PPH: FBC and ferritin. Postpartum thyroiditis: TSH. Hair shedding at 2–4 months is common (telogen effluvium).

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Wickramasinghe? It’s Dr Brennan. Is Anya with you and is now a good time? The health visitor said she’d asked you to call.
model.why: Checks it is safe to talk; uses the record

model.text: Yes, she’s asleep. I’m fine, really. I’m not depressed. I’m just on my own a lot.
I’m not here to put a label on you. Tell me about being on your own — what are your days like?
Kasun works nights, sleeps in the day. I don’t know anyone. I don’t go out much. In the evenings I cry. I feel useless.
That sounds really hard. Do you still enjoy things — Anya, talking to family? How are your sleep and appetite?
Anya makes me smile. I laugh with my mother on video. I sleep when she sleeps. I eat OK.
I ask every new mum this: have you had thoughts of harming yourself, or of ending your life? Or any worries about harming Anya? Any strange experiences, like hearing things?
No, never. She is my everything.
Who is supporting you? Is there family nearby?
My mother was going to come — it’s our custom. Her visa was refused. I feel I’m doing it alone.
I’m so sorry — that’s a real loss. Sometimes people worry about what happens if they tell a doctor they’re struggling. Is anything like that on your mind?
Will they take my baby? Will it be a problem for our visa?
No. Asking for help doesn’t lead to babies being taken away — Anya is clearly loved and doing well. And seeing us doesn’t affect your visa; you’re fully entitled to NHS care.

I don’t think you’re depressed right now. I think you’re adjusting to huge changes, mostly alone. Can we build some support? Baby groups at the Family Hub, a breastfeeding group where feeding is easy, a Home-Start volunteer who visits, and a link worker who knows local Sri Lankan and Buddhist groups. Talking to someone through NHS Talking Therapies could help too. And could Kasun know how you feel?
model.why: Working formulation and practical shared plan

model.text: Yes. I would like the groups. I will tell Kasun.

You also haven’t had your own postnatal check — let’s book it with a blood test for iron and thyroid, and talk about contraception. I’ll call you in two weeks. If you ever feel hopeless, think of harming yourself, or feel you can’t cope, call us or 111 and choose the mental health option — 999 in an emergency. What will you do first?
Tell Kasun, wait for the link worker, book my check — and call if I feel worse.

social.t: Recent arrivals often lack the family networks they expected; night-shift work in care leaves partners isolated in the day as well.
A postnatal rest period with female relatives is common in many cultures; ask what she expected rather than assuming.

legal.t: Immigration health surcharge payers have NHS access on the same basis as residents; health information is not shared with immigration authorities for routine care.
Concern for a parent’s mental health is not itself a safeguarding referral; act if a child is at risk of harm.

professional.t: Feed back the plan to the health visitor and agree joint follow-up.

community.t: Family Hub; breastfeeding peer support; Home-Start; social prescribing link worker; local temple and Sri Lankan community groups; PANDAS Foundation; NHS Talking Therapies.

playbook.diagnosis: Adjustment reaction with social isolation after childbirth and migration; no current depressive disorder or risk; raised risk of postnatal depression.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You’re not depressed at the moment — you’re coping with big changes on your own, and that’s why you feel tearful and low in the evenings.”

management.reflectIce: “You came to show me you’re coping — and you are. You also deserve support, and getting it won’t put Anya or your visa at risk.”
management.psychosocial: Tell Kasun; social prescriber; cultural community; baby and breastfeeding groups; Home-Start.
sharedPlan: Health visitor listening visits; HV review in 2 weeks
Postnatal check with FBC, ferritin, TSH; contraception
safetyNet: Hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, thoughts of harming Anya, or not coping — GP same day or NHS 111 mental health option

pitfalls.intro: Candidates either diagnose postnatal depression from the EPDS and offer an SSRI, or accept “I’m fine” and end the call.

items.fail: Skips the risk questions because she says she is fine.
items.why: Perinatal suicide and infanticide risk must always be assessed directly.
items.fix: Ask kindly and directly about self-harm, harm to the baby and psychotic symptoms.

items.why: She does not meet criteria for depression; support and therapy are first-line for an adjustment reaction.
items.fix: Practical support, talking therapy, follow-up and safety-net.

items.fail: Never discovers her fear about social services and visas.
items.why: The fear drives minimisation and will block future help-seeking.
items.fix: Ask what worries her about talking to doctors, and reassure accurately.

timeMap.d: Safe to talk? Use the HV note.
Days, mood, enjoyment, sleep, appetite, risk, bonding, support, mother’s visa.
Social services and visas — accurate reassurance.
Formulation; groups, Home-Start, link worker, Talking Therapies, Kasun.
Postnatal check and bloods, follow-up, safety-net, teach-back.

wordPics.clearFail: Accepts “I’m fine” without a mood or risk assessment, or diagnoses depression from the EPDS and prescribes an antidepressant; no follow-up.
wordPics.fail: Assesses mood and risk but misses the isolation and the fear about authorities, or gives a list of leaflets without a plan.
wordPics.pass: Assesses mood and risk thoroughly, identifies isolation and the loss of expected support, explains an adjustment reaction, offers practical and talking-therapy support, arranges follow-up and safety-nets.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus: uncovers and addresses the fear about social services and visas, explores her cultural expectations respectfully, includes her own postnatal check and bloods, involves Kasun and the health visitor, and confirms the plan by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “In your culture, mothers stay in — so that’s normal.”
avoid.instead: “What did you expect the first months to be like?”

avoid.dont: “If things get worse we may need to involve social services.”

avoid.why: Removes the barrier to honest disclosure.
